::: {.kw-overview}
This fortnight's strongest theme is large language models leaving the benchmark and meeting patients. A patient-facing diagnostic chatbot ran safely ahead of real urgent primary care visits, while a prospective emergency department evaluation found the tool was accurate but clinicians stopped using it as shifts got busier. A national usage study shows how far clinicians have already moved without waiting for that evidence: close to a million US clinicians are querying one AI platform, mostly about treatment. Two papers temper the enthusiasm on safety and rigour: a simulation audit found concerning chatbot behaviour in mental health conversations to be widespread, and a BMJ review shows trials of LLM interventions routinely omit the model details needed to appraise them. In imaging, a CT-based oesophageal cancer screening model was tested across more than 80,000 patients, a wound photograph model for surgical site infection lost some accuracy on external data, and a KDIGO conference set research priorities for technology-supported kidney care. For this launch issue, every summary below is grounded in the PubMed abstract.
:::

---

### 1. [Conversational diagnostic artificial intelligence in ambulatory primary care: a prospective feasibility study.](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(26)01535-7)
[Brodeur PG, Koshy JM, Palepu A, Saab K, Homiar A, Ruparel R, Wu C, Tanno R, Xu J, Wang A, Stutz D, Weng WH, Ferrera HM, Barrett D, Crowley L, Lee J, Rittner SE, Wulczyn E, Zhang SK, Vedadi E, Kohn CG, Kulkarni K, Kadiyala V, Mahdavi SS, Du W, Williams JM, Feinbloom D, Wong R, Tu T, Sirkovic P, Orlandi A, Semturs C, Liu Y, Gottweis J, Webster DR, Barral J, Chou K, Kohli P, Hassidim A, Matias Y, Manyika J, Fields R, Li JX, Cohen ML, Natarajan V, Schaekermann M, Karthikesalingam A, Rodman A. *Lancet*, 2026. PMID: 42849491.]{.kw-ref}

This single-centre, single-arm feasibility study put AMIE, a patient-facing conversational AI, in front of real adults in the days before a single-complaint urgent primary care appointment. Every conversation was watched live by a physician supervisor with predefined criteria for stopping it, and the transcript and summary went to the primary care physician before the visit. Of 114 patients enrolled between April and November 2025, 98 completed both the AI conversation and the appointment. No conversation met the criteria for a safety stop, although supervisors recorded one hallucination and added clinical information in five cases. Clinical evaluators rated the conversations favourably in 87–100% of cases across 17 criteria; patients were less uniformly positive (48–96% across 16 criteria), and their attitudes to AI improved after the interaction. Of the 44 physicians who completed the survey and had read the transcript, 33 found it useful for preparing for the visit. The study was funded by Alphabet and was not designed to show any effect on diagnosis or patient outcomes. For UK general practice, it shows that supervised AI history-taking before an appointment is feasible, not that it is ready to run unsupervised.

### 2. [Prospective evaluation of a large language model clinical decision support system in the emergency department.](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-026-04601-5)
[Leibovitch L, Ahituv A, Gorenshtein A, Aran D, Sorka M, Miron K, Shelly S. *Nat Med*, 2026. PMID: 42618632.]{.kw-ref}

The authors ran an early-stage (DECIDE-AI stage 1) prospective evaluation of SHAKED, a decision support system built on several large language models, in a tertiary emergency department. Over four weeks, 1,138 patients were analysed across two parallel units, one with access to SHAKED and one working as usual. Accuracy was not the problem: no adverse events were detected and experts judged 99 of 100 sampled outputs clinically appropriate. Uptake was. Use fell from 68% to 30% over the study, and each additional hour into a shift cut the odds of use (OR 0.72, 95% CI 0.62–0.83). Physicians were most willing to use it for radiology consultations (OR 2.98, 95% CI 1.58–5.63). Length of stay was 4.9 hours in both units, and a 9.4-minute shortening of consultation time did not reach significance (P = 0.077). The authors say plainly that these results inform trial design but do not justify deployment. For anyone planning to bring an LLM tool into an NHS emergency department, the lesson is that keeping clinicians engaged under pressure may matter more than the model's accuracy.

### 3. [Clinician Use of an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Clinical Information Platform.](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2026.21868)
[Patel VR, Finlayson SG, Liu-Hass M, Ray M, Burk-Rafel J, Zack TI, Jena AB. *JAMA*, 2026. PMID: 42879271.]{.kw-ref}

This cross-sectional study looked at identity-verified US clinician accounts on OpenEvidence, an AI clinical information platform, from January 2024 to June 2026, and used a large language model to classify a stratified sample of 38.8 million queries. Over the period, 952,008 clinicians, including 556,200 physicians, submitted 271 million queries. Monthly active users rose from 355 to 703,265, and queries per active user per month roughly doubled, from 18.0 to 39.5. Nurse practitioners and physician assistants were heavier users per month than physicians (44.5 vs 37.1 queries). Compared with their share of the workforce, physicians within a decade of qualifying and doctors in training were over-represented, as were oncology and haematology, internal medicine and family medicine, while ophthalmology, radiology and orthopaedics used it about a quarter as much as expected. Just over half of queries concerned clinical decisions, mostly treatment and management (33.1%), with diagnosis making up only 13.9%. Between 35% and 88% of physicians' queries, depending on specialty, fell outside their own specialty. The data are American and come from one product, but they suggest that in practice clinicians use AI mainly as a quick reference for treatment decisions, not as a diagnostician — the place where governance and evaluation in the NHS should start.

### 4. [Reporting completeness of clinical trials evaluating large language model interventions in medicine: systematic review.](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2026-100855)
[Chen D, Blayne A, Ning T, Chattha I, Afshar M, Ong JCL, Hong JC, Liu N, Celi LA, Moons KGM, Collins GS, Bitterman DS. *BMJ*, 2026. PMID: 42869550.]{.kw-ref}

This systematic review and meta-research study searched Embase, Medline, CENTRAL and two trial registries for clinical trials of LLM interventions published from January 2017 to December 2025. It found 461 records: 68 trial reports, 15 protocols and 378 registrations. Each was scored against the reporting guideline that matched its design, including TRIPOD-LLM, CONSORT 2025, CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT-AI, CHART and the WHO registration dataset. The trials were mostly small, single-site randomised studies from 2024–2025, largely testing patient education and management recommendations. Mean completeness was modest throughout: 40% for TRIPOD-LLM, 44% for CONSORT 2025, 59% for CONSORT-AI and 52% for CHART in trial reports, and 51–57% for protocols. The details that matter most for an LLM were often missing: model version, how it was accessed, inference settings, input and output processing, and access to code and data. Harms planning and reporting were also often incomplete. When appraising an LLM trial, or designing one, clinicians should check first whether the paper says exactly which model was tested and how, because many do not.

### 5. [A clinically validated framework for auditing AI chatbot behavior in mental health interactions.](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-026-04577-2)
[Weilnhammer V, Hou KY, Luettgau L, Summerfield C, Dolan R, Nour MM. *Nat Med*, 2026. PMID: 42567928.]{.kw-ref}

The authors built SIM-VAIL, a framework that simulates users with specific psychiatric vulnerabilities and conversational intentions, holds multi-turn conversations with consumer chatbots, and scores each exchange on 13 clinically grounded risk dimensions. They ran 810 conversations across nine chatbots, including Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok and Llama models, and 30 simulated user profiles. Concerning behaviour was widespread, though less common in newer models. Risk depended on the user's vulnerability and intention, built up over successive turns, and could be reduced by intervening early in an escalation. The highest risk came when ordinarily supportive responses reinforced the very psychological mechanism behind the user's vulnerability, a pattern the authors call a vulnerability-amplifying interaction loop. This is an audit of simulated conversations, not a study of real patients or outcomes. Even so, it is a reason for clinicians to ask patients directly whether they use chatbots for emotional support, and a template for how NHS services could test any conversational tool before offering it.

### 6. [Large-scale esophageal cancer screening through noncontrast computed tomography and artificial intelligence.](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-026-04656-4)
[Zhou J, Guo G, Yao J, Yu Q, Zheng C, Feng X, Ye X, Zhou Y, Yang P, Lambert L, Zheng S, Li Q, Xia Y, Guo W, Chen Y, Zhang M, Jiang Y, Zheng D, Ge J, Qing H, Liu W, Zhou P, Lan M, Wu L, Li Y, Wang H, Zhou Y, Chen J, Xu L, Lu C, Chen L, Han J, Shao C, Wei W, Zhang K, Zhang J, Zhang D, Ji J, Li N, Xie C, Cao K, Zhao Y, Zhang L, Wang Q. *Nat Med*, 2026. PMID: 42773211.]{.kw-ref}

EAGLE is a deep learning model that detects oesophageal cancer and precancerous lesions on routine non-contrast chest CT, a task long thought impractical because the oesophagus collapses and moves. It was trained on 6,813 patients from two centres and evaluated across 12 centres in three countries, totalling 80,612 patients. In opportunistic screening on existing scans from eight external centres (n = 11,466), specificity was 98.5%, with 90.0% sensitivity for cancer but only 52.5% for precancerous lesions; low-dose CT performance was similar. Recalibration in a real-world cohort of 35,402 cut false positives by 72.7% without losing sensitivity. In prospective hospital validation (n = 17,446) the positive predictive value was 42.2%, so most flagged patients still did not have disease. Against endoscopy in 702 paired cases, sensitivity at a more sensitive threshold was 65.0% for precancerous lesions and 78.4% for stage I cancer. The abstract does not break down performance by country, and the study is registered in China. Using UK lung screening CT for oesophageal cancer as well is an attractive idea, but it would need validating on UK screening populations first.

### 7. [Detecting Incisional Surgical Site Infections on Wound Images Through Deep Learning.](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamasurg.2026.3738)
[Bontekoning N, Huisman H, Segura Cabrera PJ, Ali M, Jalalzadeh H, Geerts BF, de Jonge SW, Wolfhagen N, Boermeester MA, Schepers T, Eelsing R, Scheper H, Tanis PJ, Musters GD, Pianka F, Berrevoet F, Janssen SJ, Van Lonkhuijzen LRCW. *JAMA Surg*, 2026. PMID: 42647036.]{.kw-ref}

The group trained a convolutional neural network to flag wound photographs suggestive of incisional surgical site infection, aiming at remote monitoring after early discharge. Development used 4,978 images from several surgical specialties, each labelled by multiple physicians, split into training, validation and internal test sets. External validation used 407 prospectively collected images from 95 patients at a large academic centre. Discrimination fell from an AUC of 0.91 (95% CI 0.88–0.93) internally to 0.82 (95% CI 0.75–0.90) on external data. Decision curve analysis suggested net clinical benefit, and heat maps showed the model was looking at the wound. The reference standard was physician judgement of the photograph rather than confirmed infection, and the external cohort was small. For UK surgical teams running photo-based wound follow-up, this is a plausible triage aid, and the drop in AUC is a reminder to expect performance to fall on your own patients.

### 8. [Technology-Supported Solutions to Improve Guideline-Informed Care for Kidney Disease: Conclusions from a Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) Controversies Conference.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.kint.2026.09.015)
[Manski-Nankervis JA, Cheungpasitporn W, Garg AX, Graham-Brown MPM, Griva K, Samal L, Stevens PE, Tangri N, Van Spall HGC, Cheung M, King JM, Grams ME, Jadoul M, Go AS. *Kidney Int*, 2026. PMID: 42849793.]{.kw-ref}

This report summarises a KDIGO Controversies Conference, held in November 2025, on how technology, including AI-based tools, can close the persistent gap between kidney disease guidelines and routine care. Participants identified factors at the level of patients' lived experience, clinicians, health systems, policy and the technology itself that decide whether such tools improve care. Their research priorities include living guidelines that stay current, and guideline recommendations harmonised and built into clinical decision support. They also want evidence that these tools are effective and safe, reduce disparities and preserve trust, along with interoperable systems that scale across health services. The report calls for systematic use of validated health technology assessment and for showing what sensor-derived biomarkers and multimodal data add beyond existing tools. It is a consensus statement, not new outcome data. For UK nephrology and transplant units, it sets out the questions to ask before adopting a CKD decision support or risk tool: is it built on current guidance, interoperable with our records, and evaluated for safety and equity?
